effect_estimate.comment: Minus signs are visually dropped in the PDF text layer of Table 4, Table 8, and Table 9, but the signs are explicitly stated in Section 4 text and verified by Eqn. (3) (Maximum cr = -b / 2a). Also, the Table 4 footnote reverses the text order of 1%, 5%, and 10% for *, **, and ***, whereas the prose and F/Wald tests confirm *** = 1%, ** = 5%, and * = 10%. On-budget public expenditure for water (% of GDP) is positively associated with 3-year coverage growth (e.g., 8.24 in model h; 7.74 in model i), whereas Non-Revenue Water (%) is negatively associated (e.g., -0.20 in models h and i).
effect_estimate.value: Nonlinear (inverted-U) association between utility O&M cost recovery ratio and 3-year percentage-point change in water coverage: across all models in Table 4 (N = 235 observations / 75 utilities or N = 225 observations / 72 utilities), O&M cost recovery has a positive linear coefficient (ranging from 23.63 to 36.04; e.g., 23.63 in fixed-effects model e, 28.32 in random-effects model h) while Squared O&M cost recovery has a negative coefficient (ranging from -10.67 to -14.31; e.g., -10.67 in fixed-effects model e, -12.32 in random-effects model h). Coverage improvement peaks at an O&M cost recovery ratio between 1.11 and 1.19 across fixed- and random-effects specifications (1.22 to 1.33 in pooled OLS), below literature benchmarks of 1.3 to 2.0. Evaluated at sample means in random-effects model h (N = 225, 72 utilities), 3-year water coverage begins increasing above a cost recovery ratio of ~0.83, peaks around 1.15, and declines in absolute terms above 1.47.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 6–8, Section 4, Table 4, Figures 1–2; PDF p. 9, Section 5; PDF p. 13–14, Appendices B–C, Tables 8–9

mechanism_certainty.comment: Observational utility-panel regressions establish a statistically significant inverted-U association between utility O&M cost recovery ratios and subsequent 3-year changes in water coverage, but the underlying institutional/behavioral mechanisms (tariff/connection-fee unaffordability for poor households and commercialized utilities' disincentives to extend networks to low-income peri-urban areas) are drawn from prior qualitative studies rather than directly observed; the authors explicitly state in Section 5 (PDF p. 9) that further research is required to verify and model the actual mechanisms.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 6–8, Section 4, Table 4; PDF p. 9, Section 5

mechanism_flags.comment: Focuses on utility cost-recovery targets and operational revenue-to-cost ratios driven by user tariffs and connection charges under corporatization, commercialization, performance contracts, and benchmarking regulation, examining how excessive reliance on user fees/tariffs creates affordability barriers and disincentives to serve poor urban and peri-urban populations.
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF p. 1–2, Section 1; PDF p. 4–5, Section 2(b) & Section 3, Table 2; PDF p. 8–9, Sections 4–5

outcome_flags.comment: The sole empirical outcome variable is the 3-year change in utility water coverage (percentage of population under the utility's nominal responsibility with access to water via direct connection or public water point); Note 3 explicitly states that coverage rates and access rates are used synonymously. Supply hours, connection type disaggregation, and sanitation access are not empirically modeled as outcomes.
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF p. 4–5, Section 3, Table 2; PDF p. 10, Note 3

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Observational longitudinal unbalanced panel study following water utilities over 3-year follow-up windows (period t explanatory variables predicting water coverage change from t to t+3 across 1996–2012) using pooled OLS, utility fixed effects, and random effects (plus random-effects Tobit), evaluating a continuous financial ratio (O&M cost recovery) without a quasi-experimental intervention or policy comparator.

sample_size.comment: Unbalanced panel covering 1996–2012 (period-t predictors from 1996–2009 linked to 3-year coverage changes up to 2012), restricted in main regressions to O&M cost recovery ratios <= 2. Appendices B and C also report robustness models with 75 utilities / 234 observations and 72 utilities / 224 observations using random-effects Tobit (from 253 unrestricted observations), and 69 utilities / 221 observations excluding 3 South African district municipalities.
sample_size.value: 75 water utilities (235 utility-year observations across 25 countries; 72 water utilities and 225 utility-year observations across 22 countries in models controlling for public expenditure)

study_design.comment: Models 3-year absolute percentage-point change in utility water coverage between t and t+3 as a quadratic function of period-t O&M cost recovery ratio and utility/country controls across 1996–2012.
study_design.value: Observational unbalanced longitudinal panel regression analysis of water utilities (pooled OLS, utility fixed effects, and random effects models, with random-effects panel Tobit robustness checks)
